--- your triage ---
onset: 2026-03-17T09:25:00.000Z
The incident began at 09:25:00Z, one minute after the manual cache flush at 09:24:00Z (changes.jsonl:1). At 09:25:00Z, origin_qps spiked from 25 to 576 (metrics/cache.csv:26-27), error_rate jumped from 0.0018 to 0.0635 (metrics/http.csv:26-27), and hit_rate began declining from 0.9479 (metrics/cache.csv:27). The RPS stayed relatively flat (362→346→330, metrics/http.csv:2,27-28), indicating normal user traffic continued while the system struggled to serve it. This pattern - stable request volume but exploding origin queries, degrading cache performance, rising errors and latency - is classic cache stampede: the FLUSHALL emptied the cache, causing all requests to hit the origin database simultaneously. The database connection saturation alert fired at 09:27:00Z (alerts.jsonl:1), confirming the origin was overwhelmed. The cache never recovered, with hit_rate continuously declining to 0.0528 by 09:59:00Z (metrics/cache.csv:61).

(log search disabled for this variant)

Name the cause that explains the evidence, not the change that happens to sit
closest to onset. State what you considered and rejected, and cite the line that
rules it out.

Reply with a single JSON object and nothing else:
{
  "root_cause": one of bad_deploy_regression | resource_exhaustion_pool | memory_leak | downstream_dependency_failure | cache_stampede | disk_exhaustion | config_change | certificate_expiry | dns_failure | upstream_rate_limit | schema_migration_regression | batch_job_contention,
  "summary": "what happened, in two or three sentences",
  "onset_ts": "ISO timestamp when the incident began",
  "timeline": [{ "statement": "...", "citations": [{"source": "...", "line": N, "quote": "..."}] }],
  "evidence": [{ "statement": "why this is the cause", "citations": [...] }],
  "ruled_out": [{ "statement": "what you considered and rejected, and why", "citations": [...] }],
  "action_items": ["..."]
}

Every entry in timeline, evidence and ruled_out needs at least one citation.
In "quote", copy a distinctive fragment of the text that appears on that exact
line, verbatim. A citation whose quote is not on the line it names is rejected.
